o: **Understanding the problem**: Count triples of 1-cells forming a right angle: one cell shares its row with a second and its column with a third. For a 1-cell at (i, j), any choice of another 1 in row i and another 1 in column j forms a triangle with (i, j) as the corner — the other two cells need not see each other. So the count is Σ over 1-cells of (rowOnes[i] − 1) × (colOnes[j] − 1). Example 1: center-column cells each contribute → total 2.
k: Each right triangle has a unique corner cell; counting per-corner avoids double counting.
Precompute row and column 1-counts once; the answer is a single pass over the grid.

a.i: rowCnt[i] and colCnt[j] give the number of 1s sharing the corner's row/column; excluding the corner itself leaves (rowCnt−1)(colCnt−1) triangles per 1-cell.
s: Compute rowCnt for every row and colCnt for every column.
For each cell equal to 1, add (rowCnt[i] − 1) × (colCnt[j] − 1) to the answer.
a.t: O(m·n) — two counting passes and one accumulation pass
a.sp: O(m + n) — the row and column count arrays

w: **Wrap-up**: The unique-corner observation collapses a seemingly combinatorial problem into arithmetic. Pitfalls: subtracting 1 correctly (the corner itself must not be counted as its own arm), and overflow — with 1000×1000 all-ones the answer is 10¹²·… far beyond 32 bits, so use long/BigInt-safe types. Follow-ups: count triangles in 3D grids, or weight cells and sum weights of corners.
